claim: Tail-anchored (TA) proteins insert post-translationally into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and peroxisomes.
source: Tail-anchored (TA) proteins insert post-translationally into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and peroxisomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about TA protein targeting in the field.

claim: The GET pathway controls ER-targeting of TA proteins.
source: Whereas the GET pathway controls ER-targeting, no dedicated factors are known for OMM insertion, posing the question of how accuracy is achieved.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about the GET pathway function.

claim: No dedicated factors are known for OMM insertion of TA proteins.
source: Whereas the GET pathway controls ER-targeting, no dedicated factors are known for OMM insertion, posing the question of how accuracy is achieved.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The mitochondrial AAA-ATPase Msp1 removes mislocalized TA proteins from the OMM.
source: The mitochondrial AAA-ATPase Msp1 removes mislocalized TA proteins from the OMM, but it is unclear, how Msp1 clients are targeted for degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, as indicated by the context.

claim: The ER-associated degradation (ERAD) E3 ubiquitin ligase Doa10 controls cytoplasmic level of Msp1 clients.
source: We show that the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) E3 ubiquitin ligase Doa10 controls cytoplasmic level of Msp1 clients.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The uncharacterized OMM protein Fmp32 is a native client for Msp1 and Doa10.
source: Furthermore, we identified the uncharacterized OMM protein Fmp32 and the ectopically expressed subunit of the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) complex Gem1 as native clients for Msp1 and Doa10.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Gem1, a subunit of the ERMES complex, is a native client for Msp1 and Doa10.
source: Furthermore, we identified the uncharacterized OMM protein Fmp32 and the ectopically expressed subunit of the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) complex Gem1 as native clients for Msp1 and Doa10.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Productive localization of TA proteins to the OMM is ensured by complex assembly.
source: We propose that productive localization of TA proteins to the OMM is ensured by complex assembly, while orphan subunits are extracted by Msp1 and eventually degraded by Doa10.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Orphan subunits of TA protein complexes are extracted by Msp1 and degraded by Doa10.
source: We propose that productive localization of TA proteins to the OMM is ensured by complex assembly, while orphan subunits are extracted by Msp1 and eventually degraded by Doa10.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The signal recognition particle (SRP) recognizes N-terminal signal sequences of ER-targeted nascent polypeptides.
source: The signal recognition particle (SRP) recognizes N-terminal signal sequences of ER-targeted nascent polypeptides and recruits the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the Sec61 translocon (Voorhees and Hegde, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SRP recruits the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the Sec61 translocon.
source: The signal recognition particle (SRP) recognizes N-terminal signal sequences of ER-targeted nascent polypeptides and recruits the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the Sec61 translocon (Voorhees and Hegde, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TA proteins have a single transmembrane (TM) domain at their very C-terminus.
source: Tail-anchored (TA) proteins are a specific class of membrane proteins that have a single transmembrane (TM) domain at their very C-terminus.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of TA proteins, representing established knowledge.

claim: TA proteins are involved in various cellular processes such as membrane fusion, protein translocation and regulation of apoptosis.
source: They are involved in various cellular processes such as membrane fusion, protein translocation and regulation of apoptosis (Antonsson, 2001; Beilharz et al., 2003; Burri and Lithgow, 2004; Chen and Scheller, 2001; Kalbfleisch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A cytosolic pre-targeting complex comprising Sgt2, Get4, and Get5 captures the TM segment of a TA protein after it emerges from the ribosome.
source: In brief, a cytosolic pre-targeting complex comprising Sgt2, Get4, and Get5 captures the TM segment of a TA protein after it emerges from the ribosome and loads it onto Get3 (Mariappan et al., 2010; Mateja et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GET pathway supported by citations.

claim: The pre-targeting complex loads the TA protein onto Get3.
source: In brief, a cytosolic pre-targeting complex comprising Sgt2, Get4, and Get5 captures the TM segment of a TA protein after it emerges from the ribosome and loads it onto Get3 (Mariappan et al., 2010; Mateja et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GET pathway supported by citations.

claim: Get3 is recruited to the ER membrane via the Get1-Get2 receptor complex.
source: This cytosolic ATPase targeting factor is subsequently recruited to the ER membrane via the Get1-Get2 receptor complex where, after ATP hydrolysis, the TA protein is inserted into the membrane (Mariappan et al., 2011; Schuldiner et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GET pathway supported by citations.

claim: After ATP hydrolysis by Get3, the TA protein is inserted into the ER membrane.
source: This cytosolic ATPase targeting factor is subsequently recruited to the ER membrane via the Get1-Get2 receptor complex where, after ATP hydrolysis, the TA protein is inserted into the membrane (Mariappan et al., 2011; Schuldiner et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GET pathway supported by citations.

claim: The EMC complex ensures ER targeting of a subset of TA proteins in mammalian cells.
source: Recently, the EMC complex (ER membrane protein complex) was shown to ensure ER targeting of a subset of TA proteins in mammalian cells (Guna et al., 2018).
evidence: This is recent knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: It is unclear how TA proteins insert into the OMM lipid bilayer.
source: However, no dedicated pathway targeting TA proteins to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) has been identified so far and it is unclear how they insert into the lipid bilayer (Vitali et al., 2018).
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge in the field supported by a citation.

claim: TA proteins can insert unassisted into the OMM due to its low ergosterol content.
source: From in vitro studies, it has been proposed that because of the low ergosterol content of the OMM TA proteins can insert unassisted (Kemper et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from in vitro studies supported by a citation.

claim: In yeast, three major branches of ERAD are centered around the polytopic E3 ubiquitin ligases Hrd1, Doa10 and Asi1/3.
source: In yeast, three major branches of ERAD are centered around the polytopic E3 ubiquitin ligases Hrd1, Doa10 and Asi1/3 (Bays et al., 2001; Carvalho et al., 2006; Deak and Wolf, 2001; Foresti et al., 2014; Khmelinskii et al., 2014; Swanson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERAD pathways supported by citations.

claim: Hrd1 is specific for proteins with misfolded ER luminal or aberrant TM domains.
source: While Hrd1 is specific for proteins with misfolded ER luminal or aberrant TM domains, Doa10 primarily mediates degradation of ER proteins with cytosolic lesions (Carvalho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERAD substrate specificity supported by a citation.

claim: Doa10 primarily mediates degradation of ER proteins with cytosolic lesions.
source: While Hrd1 is specific for proteins with misfolded ER luminal or aberrant TM domains, Doa10 primarily mediates degradation of ER proteins with cytosolic lesions (Carvalho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERAD substrate specificity supported by a citation.

claim: The Asi1/3 complex removes misfolded or mislocalized membrane proteins from the inner nuclear membrane.
source: The Asi1/3 complex removes misfolded or mislocalized membrane proteins from the inner nuclear membrane, a sub-area of the ER (Foresti et al., 2014; Khmelinskii et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Asi complex function supported by citations.

claim: Doa10 triggers degradation of proteins with hydrophobic sequences at either end of the protein.
source: In this context, Doa10 triggers degradation of proteins with hydrophobic sequences at either end of the protein, such as hydrophobic C-terminal pro-domains of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins (Ast et al., 2014) or hydrophobic N-termini (Kats et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Doa10 substrate specificity supported by citations.

claim: The AAA-ATPase Cdc48 provides energy for retro-translocation and extraction of membrane-embedded ERAD substrates.
source: For retro-translocation and extraction of membrane-embedded ERAD substrates the required energy is provided by the AAA-ATPase Cdc48 (Ye et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cdc48 function supported by a citation.

claim: Cdc48 substrate recognition is mediated through its Ufd1-Npl4 cofactor, which binds ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Cdc48 substrate recognition is mediated through its Ufd1-Npl4 cofactor, which binds ubiquitinated proteins (Meyer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cdc48 cofactor function supported by a citation.

claim: Ubx2 binds to the TOM complex, defining a mitochondrial protein translocation-associated degradation pathway.
source: Likewise, Ubx2 which was thought to be an ERAD-specific Cdc48 adaptor, has been shown to also bind to the TOM (translocase of the outer membrane) complex, defining a mitochondrial protein translocation-associated degradation pathway (Mårtensson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is recent knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Doa1 or Vms1 recruit the Cdc48 complex to OMM-anchored ubiquitinated proteins for proteasomal degradation.
source: In a related process referred to as mitochondria-associated degradation, Doa1 or Vms1 recruit the Cdc48 complex to OMM-anchored ubiquitinated proteins to target them for proteasomal degradation (Anton et al., 2011; Heo et al., 2010; Karbowski and Youle, 2011; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondria-associated degradation supported by citations.

claim: Msp1 shows dual localization to the OMM and peroxisomes.
source: Whereas this pathway is linked to the ubiquitin-proteasome system through the cytoplasmic E3 ubiquitin ligases Rsp5 and Mdm30, an alternative extraction mechanism relies on the AAA-ATPase Msp1 (known as ATAD1/Thorase in humans). Msp1 shows dual localization to the OMM and peroxisomes (Chen et al., 2014; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Msp1 localization supported by citations.

claim: Pex15 evades Msp1-dependent extraction by interacting with other peroxisomal proteins such as Pex3.
source: In peroxisomes it has been suggested, that the TA protein Pex15 evades Msp1-dependent extraction by interacting with other peroxisomal proteins such as Pex3 (Weir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Deletion of Msp1 leads to stabilization of mistargeted peroxisomal Pex15 or the Golgi v-SNARE Gos1 in the OMM.
source: Deletion of Msp1 leads to stabilization of mistargeted peroxisomal Pex15 or the Golgi v-SNARE Gos1 in the OMM (Chen et al., 2014; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Msp1 is sufficient to extract TA proteins from proteoliposomes in vitro.
source: In vitro studies suggest that Msp1 is sufficient to extract TA proteins from proteoliposomes (Wohlever et al., 2017).
evidence: This is knowledge from in vitro studies supported by a citation.

claim: The Msp1 N-terminal TM domain is dispensable for the dislocation reaction in vitro.
source: Although these reconstitution experiments showed that the Msp1 N-terminal TM domain is dispensable for the dislocation reaction, recently Li et al. suggested that a conserved negatively charged aspartate residue in the N-terminal portion of Msp1 facing the inter membrane space (IMS) is important for efficient recognition of Msp1 clients in vivo (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is knowledge from in vitro studies supported by a citation.

claim: A conserved negatively charged aspartate residue in the N-terminal portion of Msp1 facing the IMS is important for efficient recognition of Msp1 clients in vivo.
source: Although these reconstitution experiments showed that the Msp1 N-terminal TM domain is dispensable for the dislocation reaction, recently Li et al. suggested that a conserved negatively charged aspartate residue in the N-terminal portion of Msp1 facing the inter membrane space (IMS) is important for efficient recognition of Msp1 clients in vivo (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is recent knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: A hydrophobic surface of the AAA-ATPase domain has been implicated in recognition of Msp1 clients.
source: Moreover, a hydrophobic surface of the AAA-ATPase domain has been implicated in recognition of Msp1 clients (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: No clear sequence consensus between all known Msp1 clients exists.
source: However, no clear sequence consensus between all known Msp1 clients exists (Chen et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Okreglak and Walter, 2014) and the mechanism how Msp1 distinguishes between mislocalized and properly located TA proteins is ill defined.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: Cis1 can recruit Msp1 to TOM for degradation of stalled import intermediates.
source: This, taken together with the finding that Cis1 can recruit Msp1 to TOM for degradation of stalled import intermediates (Weidberg and Amon, 2018), indicates that multiple routes can target proteins for Msp1-mediated dislocation.
evidence: This is knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Wild type Pex15 localizes to peroxisomes.
source: Whereas wild type (wt) Pex15 localizes to peroxisomes, Pex15Δ30 constitutively mislocalizes to the OMM and exhibits Msp1-dependent turnover (Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Pex15Δ30 constitutively mislocalizes to the OMM and exhibits Msp1-dependent turnover.
source: Whereas wild type (wt) Pex15 localizes to peroxisomes, Pex15Δ30 constitutively mislocalizes to the OMM and exhibits Msp1-dependent turnover (Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: GFP-Pex15Δ30 localized predominantly to mitochondria and only to a minor extent to peroxisomes in wt and msp1Δ cells.
source: Pex15Δ30 N-terminally tagged with the circular permuted cp8 superfolder GFP variant (referred to GFP hereafter), which shows less cytoplasmic background due to improved proteasomal degradation (Khmelinskii et al., 2016), localized predominantly to mitochondria and only to a minor extent to peroxisomes in wt and msp1Δ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Deletion of GET3 caused a significant increase in sfGFP level and mCherry/sfGFP ratio of tFT-Pex15Δ30.
source: Moreover, deletion of GET3, which was previously linked to trafficking of full-length Pex15 and shows a negative genetic interaction with msp1Δ (Costanzo et al., 2010; Okreglak and Walter, 2014), caused a significant increase in sfGFP level and mCherry/sfGFP ratio.
evidence: This is a finding from the screen supported by data.

claim: tFT-Pex15Δ30 was significantly stabilized in the absence of Spf1, Prm1, Doa10, Ubc7, and Cue1.
source: tFT-Pex15Δ30 was also significantly stabilized in the absence of the ER-resident P-type ATPase Spf1, the pheromone regulated membrane protein Prm1 and, interestingly, the ER-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase Doa10, its associated E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme Ubc7 and its tethering factor Cue1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the screen supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Strains lacking MSP1, DOA10, UBC7, CUE1, GET3 or SPF1 showed increased sfGFP fluorescence and mCherry/sfGFP ratios compared to wt.
source: Strains lacking MSP1, DOA10, UBC7, CUE1, GET3 or SPF1 consistently showed increased sfGFP fluorescence and mCherry/sfGFP ratios compared to wt (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a validation finding supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of UBC6 stabilized tFT-Pex15Δ30.
source: Deletion of UBC6 also stabilized tFT-Pex15Δ30.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation experiments.

claim: Deletion of PRM1 did not stabilize tFT-Pex15Δ30.
source: In contrast, we did not observe stabilization of tFT-Pex15Δ30 in prm1Δ cells and excluded this mutant from further analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation experiments.

claim: In msp1Δ, doa10Δ, ubc6Δ, ubc7Δ, and get3Δ mutant strains tFT-Pex15Δ30 accumulated in mitochondrial structures.
source: In msp1Δ, doa10Δ, ubc6Δ, ubc7Δ, and get3Δ mutant strains tFT-Pex15Δ30 accumulated in mitochondrial structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Deletion of SPF1 led to pronounced ER localization of tFT-Pex15Δ30.
source: Whereas ablation of Get3 or the Doa10 complex lead to accumulation of Pex15Δ30 in mitochondria, deletion of SPF1 led to pronounced ER localization (Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by images in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mitochondrial TA proteins mislocalize to the ER in spf1Δ strains.
source: This finding is consistent with a previous report demonstrating that mitochondrial TA proteins mislocalize to the ER in spf1Δ strains (Krumpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: The overall levels of the tFT-Pex15Δ30 reporter increased in the spf1Δ mutant.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the ER localization, the overall levels of the tFT-Pex15Δ30 reporter increased in the spf1Δ mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a characteristic 26 kDa remnant of sfGFP that persists vacuolar degradation in spf1∆ cells.
source: Western blot analysis revealed a characteristic 26 kDa remnant of sfGFP that persists vacuolar degradation in spf1∆ cells (Figure 2B) (Khmelinskii et al., 2016; Shintani and Klionsky, 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 2B and citations.

claim: Deletion of Get2, Get4, or Get5 resulted in increased levels of tFT-Pex15Δ30 and accumulation in mitochondria.
source: Similar to get3Δ, deletion of the ER membrane receptor subunit Get2 or the cytosolic pre-targeting factors Get4 and Get5 resulted in increased levels of the tFT-Pex15Δ30 and accumulation in mitochondria (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and flow cytometry analysis supported by data in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Western blot analysis showed an increase of tFT-Pex15Δ30 level in a similar range as msp1Δ for all GET mutants.
source: Western blot analysis showed an increase of tFT-Pex15Δ30 level in a similar range as msp1Δ for all GET mutants (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 2E.

claim: The characteristic 26 kDa vacuolar tFT degradation intermediate observed for spf1∆ was not seen in get3Δ cells.
source: Of note, the characteristic 26 kDa vacuolar tFT degradation intermediate observed for spf1∆ was not seen in get3Δ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ubc6, Ubc7 and Doa10 are the only significant hits in the ubiquitination machinery screen for tFT-Pex15Δ30.
source: Rescreening of the tFT-Pex15Δ30 reporter against a library of mutants in the ubiquitination machinery confirmed that Ubc6, Ubc7 and Doa10 are the only significant hits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the targeted screen supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: tFT-Pex15Δ30 levels were higher in doa10Δ compared to msp1Δ.
source: Notably, tFT-Pex15Δ30 levels were higher in doa10Δ compared to msp1Δ, and further increased in the msp1Δdoa10Δ double mutant (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry and western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: tFT-Pex15Δ30 levels further increased in the msp1Δdoa10Δ double mutant.
source: Notably, tFT-Pex15Δ30 levels were higher in doa10Δ compared to msp1Δ, and further increased in the msp1Δdoa10Δ double mutant (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry and western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Fitness of the msp1Δdoa10Δ mutant was indistinguishable from wt.
source: Different to an msp1∆get3∆ double deletion, which shows a fitness defect (Chen et al., 2014; Okreglak and Walter, 2014), fitness of the msp1Δdoa10Δ mutant was indistinguishable from wt (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), excluding a general toxicity effect and pointing towards a direct role of Doa10 in Pex15Δ30 degradation.
evidence: This is a finding from growth assays supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and citations.

claim: Addition of proteasome inhibitors delayed turnover of the Pex15Δ30 reporter.
source: Consistent with ubiquitin-dependent degradation, addition of proteasome inhibitors delayed turnover of the Pex15Δ30 reporter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments with proteasome inhibitors supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Double deletion of MSP1 and DOA10 showed an additive stabilization effect of Pex15Δ30.
source: Moreover, double deletion of MSP1 and DOA10 showed an additive stabilization effect of Pex15Δ30 (Figure 3A), suggesting that the two proteins do not act in a linear pathway.
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis supported by data in Figure 3A, leading to an inference about pathway organization.

claim: Msp1 and Doa10 do not act in a linear pathway.
source: Moreover, double deletion of MSP1 and DOA10 showed an additive stabilization effect of Pex15Δ30 (Figure 3A), suggesting that the two proteins do not act in a linear pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effect observed in the double mutant.

claim: Only mitochondrial accumulation of tFT-Pex15Δ30 was observed in doa10Δ.
source: Doa10 is a major player of ERAD-C (Mehrtash and Hochstrasser, 2018; Ruggiano et al., 2014). However, we observed only mitochondrial accumulation of tFT-Pex15Δ30 in doa10Δ (Figure 3C), indicating that it acts on pre-inserted TA protein reporter.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Doa10 acts on pre-inserted TA protein reporter.
source: Doa10 is a major player of ERAD-C (Mehrtash and Hochstrasser, 2018; Ruggiano et al., 2014). However, we observed only mitochondrial accumulation of tFT-Pex15Δ30 in doa10Δ (Figure 3C), indicating that it acts on pre-inserted TA protein reporter.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that tFT-Pex15Δ30 accumulates in mitochondria in doa10Δ.

claim: Pex15Δ30 turnover was not affected in the absence of Hrd1 and Asi1/3.
source: Moreover, Pex15Δ30 turnover was not affected in the absence of Hrd1 and Asi1/3, the other two ERAD E3 ligases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the screen and cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B and C.

claim: Western blot analysis of tFT-Pex15Δ30 in doa10Δ revealed accumulation of the vacuolar tFT degradation intermediate at 26 kDa.
source: In line with this, western blot analysis of tFT-Pex15Δ30 in doa10Δ revealed accumulation of the vacuolar tFT degradation intermediate at 26 kDa (Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Khmelinskii et al., 2016; Shintani and Klionsky, 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and citations.

claim: Additional deletion of MSP1 decreased abundance of the vacuolar tFT degradation fragment in doa10Δ.
source: Interestingly, additional deletion of MSP1 decreased abundance of this fragment suggesting that mitochondria act as a 'sink' for mistargeted tFT-Pex15Δ30.
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis leading to an inference.

claim: Mitochondria act as a 'sink' for mistargeted tFT-Pex15Δ30.
source: Interestingly, additional deletion of MSP1 decreased abundance of this fragment suggesting that mitochondria act as a 'sink' for mistargeted tFT-Pex15Δ30.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the vacuolar fragment decreases when MSP1 is deleted.

claim: The vacuolar sfGFP fragment was absent in the get3Δ mutant.
source: Along this hypothesis, the vacuolar sfGFP fragment was absent in the get3Δ mutant, supporting the idea that Get3 is required for membrane insertion and subsequent transport of tFT-Pex15Δ30 to the vacuole (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Get3 is required for membrane insertion and subsequent transport of tFT-Pex15Δ30 to the vacuole.
source: Along this hypothesis, the vacuolar sfGFP fragment was absent in the get3Δ mutant, supporting the idea that Get3 is required for membrane insertion and subsequent transport of tFT-Pex15Δ30 to the vacuole (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of the vacuolar fragment in get3Δ.

claim: No prominent ER localization of tFT-Pex15Δ30 is observed in doa10Δ.
source: Since in doa10Δ no prominent ER localization is observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we assume that tFT-Pex15Δ30 only very transiently exists in the ER.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: tFT-Pex15Δ30 only very transiently exists in the ER in doa10Δ.
source: Since in doa10Δ no prominent ER localization is observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we assume that tFT-Pex15Δ30 only very transiently exists in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of prominent ER localization.

claim: Upon GET3 deletion, Ste6* showed a minor stabilization.
source: To this end, we studied turnover of the Doa10-dependent ERAD substrate Ste6* (Stolz et al., 2010). Interestingly, upon GET3 deletion Ste6* showed a minor stabilization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and a citation.

claim: Galactose induction of Msp1 in the doa10Δ background did not affect cellular tFT-Pex15Δ30 level.
source: Galactose induction of Msp1 in the doa10Δ background did not affect cellular tFT-Pex15Δ30 level, consistent with the requirement of Doa10 for degradation (Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry and cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of Msp1 in doa10Δ caused tFT-Pex15Δ30 to relocalize from mitochondria to the cytosol and the ER.
source: Fluorescence microscopy, however, revealed that tFT-Pex15Δ30 was not detected any more in mitochondria. The GFP signal changed its localization to the cytosol and the ER, whereas mCherry was only detected in the vacuole (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Overexpression of Msp1 in cue1Δ or ubc6Δ did not restore tFT-Pex15Δ30 levels to wt.
source: Likewise, overexpression of Msp1 in cue1Δ or ubc6Δ did not restore tFT-Pex15Δ30 levels to wt (Figure 4A) and imaging showed relocalization of tFT-Pex15Δ30 from mitochondria to the cytosol, the ER and the vacuole (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry and microscopy analysis supported by data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Reduced poly-ubiquitination of Pex15Δ30 was observed in the doa10∆ strain.
source: Consistent with this, we observed also reduced poly-ubiquitination of Pex15Δ30 in the doa10∆ strain (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from ubiquitination assays supported by data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In the absence of Doa10, a prominent single band resembling mono-ubiquitinated Pex15Δ30 was observed.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of Doa10 a prominent single band resembling mono-ubiquitinated Pex15Δ30 was observed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from ubiquitination assays supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: Alternative ubiquitination events not leading to proteasomal degradation can occur in the absence of Doa10.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of Doa10 a prominent single band resembling mono-ubiquitinated Pex15Δ30 was observed (Figure 4C). This indicates that alternative ubiquitination events not leading to proteasomal degradation can occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of mono-ubiquitinated Pex15Δ30 in doa10Δ.

claim: Six proteins showed a more than 2-fold increase in their GFP level upon deletion of DOA10 in the TA protein screen.
source: This screen identified six proteins with a more than 2-fold increase in their GFP level upon deletion of DOA10 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Ubc6 is a substrate of Doa10 in the context of ERAD.
source: One of them, Ubc6, had been shown to be a substrate of Doa10 in the context of ERAD (Figure 5A and B) (Walter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and confirmed by the screen data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Csm4, Pgc1, Sps2, and Ydl241w accumulated upon compromised function of Doa10.
source: Other proteins that accumulated upon compromised function of Doa10 are Csm4, Pgc1, Sps2, Ydl241w.
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen.

claim: Csm4, Pgc1, Sps2, and Ydl241w localized to the ER or other vesicular structures.
source: These proteins localized to the ER or other vesicular structures (Figure 5B) and did not accumulate in the msp1Δ mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by data in Figure 5B and Figure 5A.

claim: Csm4, Pgc1, Sps2, and Ydl241w did not accumulate in the msp1Δ mutant.
source: These proteins localized to the ER or other vesicular structures (Figure 5B) and did not accumulate in the msp1Δ mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: The strongest stabilization in doa10Δ was observed for Fmp32.
source: The strongest stabilization in doa10Δ was observed for Fmp32, which is an uncharacterized mitochondrial protein implicated in maintenance of the respiratory capacity of mitochondria (Paupe et al., 2015) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen supported by data in Figure 5A and B, and a citation.

claim: Fmp32 is an uncharacterized mitochondrial protein implicated in maintenance of the respiratory capacity of mitochondria.
source: The strongest stabilization in doa10Δ was observed for Fmp32, which is an uncharacterized mitochondrial protein implicated in maintenance of the respiratory capacity of mitochondria (Paupe et al., 2015) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Weak but significant accumulation of Pex15, Gos1 and Fmp32 was identified in msp1Δ.
source: A similar analysis in msp1Δ identified weak, but significant accumulation of 3 proteins: Pex15, Gos1 and Fmp32 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: A small fraction of full-length Pex15 and Gos1 mislocalized to mitochondria and are subject to Msp1-dependent extraction.
source: This indicates that consistent with previous reports (Chen et al., 2014), a small fraction of full-length Pex15, as well as Gos1, mislocalized to mitochondria and are subject to Msp1-dependent extraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the screen data and consistent with prior studies supported by a citation.

claim: Full-length Pex15 and Gos1 do not accumulate in DOA10 deletion strains.
source: In contrast to Pex15Δ30, full-length Pex15 and Gos1 do not accumulate in DOA10 deletion strains, indicating that in presence of active Mps1 they are efficiently targeted to their native destination.
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen.

claim: In presence of active Msp1, full-length Pex15 and Gos1 are efficiently targeted to their native destination.
source: In contrast to Pex15Δ30, full-length Pex15 and Gos1 do not accumulate in DOA10 deletion strains, indicating that in presence of active Mps1 they are efficiently targeted to their native destination.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that they do not accumulate in doa10Δ.

claim: The strongest effect of MSP1 deletion was observed for Fmp32 (1.8-fold increase).
source: Again, the strongest effect of MSP1 deletion was observed for Fmp32 (1.8-fold increase) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the TA protein screen supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: Fmp32 is extracted and degraded in a concerted action by Doa10 and Msp1.
source: This indicates that like the Pex15Δ30 reporter, Fmp32 is extracted and degraded in a concerted action by Doa10 and Msp1.
evidence: This is inferred from the screen data showing accumulation in both msp1Δ and doa10Δ.

claim: Under its native promoter, sfGFP-tagged Fmp32 is almost undetectable in wt strains.
source: Interestingly, under its native promoter, sfGFP-tagged Fmp32 is almost undetectable in wt strains (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Deletion of MSP1 led to a robust increase in the levels of sfGFP-Fmp32.
source: Deletion of MSP1 led to a robust increase in the levels of sfGFP-Fmp32 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: sfGFP-Fmp32 did not accumulate in the absence of Cis1.
source: Of note, sfGFP-Fmp32 did not accumulate in the absence of Cis1, indicating that is extracted by the canonical Msp1 activity and not target for mitochondrial protein import stress response (Weidberg and Amon, 2018) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: Fmp32 is extracted by the canonical Msp1 activity and not targeted for mitochondrial protein import stress response.
source: Of note, sfGFP-Fmp32 did not accumulate in the absence of Cis1, indicating that is extracted by the canonical Msp1 activity and not target for mitochondrial protein import stress response (Weidberg and Amon, 2018) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of accumulation in cis1Δ.

claim: Deletion of DOA10 alone or in combination with MSP1 led to a dramatic increase of Fmp32 localizing both to the cytosol and mitochondria.
source: Deletion of DOA10 alone or in combination with MSP1 led to a dramatic increase of Fmp32 localizing both to the cytosol and mitochondria (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy and western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The mitochondrial protein Fmp32 is constantly degraded by Doa10 with the assistance of Msp1 extracting it from the OMM.
source: This result implies that the mitochondrial protein Fmp32 is constantly degraded by Doa10 with the assistance of Msp1 extracting it from the OMM.
evidence: This is inferred from the dramatic accumulation of Fmp32 in doa10Δ and msp1Δdoa10Δ.

claim: Msp1 and ATP are necessary and sufficient for the extraction of TA proteins from proteoliposomes in vitro.
source: In vitro studies demonstrated that Msp1 and ATP are necessary and sufficient for the extraction of TA proteins from proteoliposomes (Wohlever et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from in vitro studies supported by a citation.

claim: Msp1 acts on its clients without co-factors.
source: Together with our screening data, which did not identify additional non-essential mitochondrial factors needed for Pex15Δ30 turnover, this suggests that Msp1 acts on its clients without co-factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro data and the lack of additional factors identified in the screen.

claim: A juxtamembrane cytoplasmic hydrophobic patch in Pex15 is important for Msp1-mediated extraction.
source: Recent analysis suggested the involvement of a juxtamembrane cytoplasmic hydrophobic patch in Pex15 is important for Msp1-mediated extraction (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Fmp32 and Gem1 do not show a juxtamembrane hydrophobic patch.
source: However, Fmp32 and Gem1 do not show this feature (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from hydrophobicity analysis supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Known Msp1 clients lack any obvious similarity in their TM anchors.
source: Since known Msp1 clients lack any obvious similarity in their TM anchors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) (Chen et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Okreglak and Walter, 2014), we asked whether sequence-independent parameters may determine specificity.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence alignment analysis supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and citations.

claim: The FRB1TMD protein localized to mitochondria.
source: The FRB1TMD protein localized to mitochondria (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: FRB1TMD fusion protein showed a half-life in the range of the Pex15Δ30 reporter.
source: Whereas FRB1TMD fusion protein showed a half-life in the range of the Pex15Δ30 reporter (Figure 3C, Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), FKBP12-Pex15TMD was more stable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 3C, Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FKBP12-Pex15TMD was more stable than FRB1TMD.
source: Whereas FRB1TMD fusion protein showed a half-life in the range of the Pex15Δ30 reporter (Figure 3C, Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), FKBP12-Pex15TMD was more stable (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The FRB1TMD reporter was degraded in an Msp1- and Doa10-dependent manner.
source: Importantly, the FRB1TMD reporter was degraded in an Msp1- and Doa10-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from steady state analysis supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Addition of rapamycin completely stabilized FRB1TMD when co-expressed with FKBP12TMD.
source: Addition of rapamycin completely stabilized FRB1TMD when co-expressed with FKBP12TMD (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) whereas no effect was observed in strains only expressing FRB1TMD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 6B, C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No effect of rapamycin was observed in strains only expressing FRB1TMD.
source: Addition of rapamycin completely stabilized FRB1TMD when co-expressed with FKBP12TMD (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) whereas no effect was observed in strains only expressing FRB1TMD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Co-expression of soluble cytoplasmic FKBP12 constructs slightly increased half-life of FRB1TMD from 12 min to 20 min.
source: In contrast, co-expression of soluble cytoplasmic FKBP12 constructs slightly increased half-life of FRB1TMD from 12 min to 20 min (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a finding from cycloheximide chase experiments supported by data in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Dimerization with a membrane integral protein counteracts Msp1 extraction and subsequent degradation of the Pex15-based reporter.
source: Taken together these results showed that dimerization with a membrane integral protein counteracts Msp1 extraction and subsequent degradation of our Pex15-based reporter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dimerization experiments.

claim: Msp1-mediated extraction is influenced by energy required for unfolding and disassembly of the cytoplasmic client domain.
source: The partial stabilization of FRB1TMD in complex with soluble FKBP12 constructs suggests that the Msp1-mediated extraction is influenced by energy required for unfolding and disassembly of the cytoplasmic client domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial stabilization observed with soluble FKBP12.

claim: Msp1 acts as unspecific extraction factor for monomeric TA proteins.
source: In conclusion, the result of the induced-dimerization experiment supports the model that Msp1 acts as unspecific extraction factor for monomeric TA proteins and, as observed in other cellular organelles, protein maturation is accompanied by formation of stable multiprotein complexes (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2018).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the dimerization experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: Protein maturation is accompanied by formation of stable multiprotein complexes.
source: In conclusion, the result of the induced-dimerization experiment supports the model that Msp1 acts as unspecific extraction factor for monomeric TA proteins and, as observed in other cellular organelles, protein maturation is accompanied by formation of stable multiprotein complexes (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Gem1 is a TA protein associated with the ERMES complex.
source: An example is Gem1, which is a TA protein associated with the ER-mitochondria-tethering complex ERMES (ER-mitochondria encounter structure) (Kornmann et al., 2011) that was not included in our TA array (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A weak but significant increase in sfGFP-Gem1 levels were detected in the msp1Δ strains.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, a weak but significant increase in sfGFP-Gem1 levels were detected in the msp1Δ strains (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Deletion of DOA10 and the msp1Δdoa10Δ mutant increased sfGFP-Gem1 levels.
source: As observed for the Pex15Δ30 reporter and Fmp32, deletion of DOA10 and the msp1Δdoa10Δ mutant increased sfGFP-Gem1 levels.
evidence: This is a finding from western blot analysis.

claim: Gem1 is a client for both Msp1 and Doa10.
source: This shows, that Gem1 is an additional client for both, Msp1 and Doa10.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the accumulation of Gem1 in msp1Δ and doa10Δ.

claim: Gem1 is only stable in presence of the other ERMES subunits.
source: Taken together with previous observation that Gem1 is only stable in presence of the other ERMES subunits (Kornmann et al., 2011), this result implies that complex formation is a primary determinant preventing extraction by Msp1.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Complex formation is a primary determinant preventing extraction by Msp1.
source: Taken together with previous observation that Gem1 is only stable in presence of the other ERMES subunits (Kornmann et al., 2011), this result implies that complex formation is a primary determinant preventing extraction by Msp1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Gem1 accumulates in msp1Δ and is only stable with other ERMES subunits.

claim: The Msp1 dislocase does not need any assistance for substrate recognition and extraction.
source: Since, we did not identify any additional factor, we suggest that the Msp1 dislocase does not need any assistance for substrate recognition and extraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additional factors identified in the genome-wide screen.

claim: The oligomeric state of TA proteins in the OMM regulates Msp1-mediated extraction.
source: We could also show that the oligomeric state of TA proteins in the OMM regulates Msp1-mediated extraction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dimerization experiments.

claim: Fmp32 and Gem1 do not show a hydrophobic juxtamembrane patch.
source: Likewise, these additional substrates do not show a hydrophobic juxtamembrane patch that recently has been suggested to be crucial for recognition of TA proteins by Msp1 (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from hydrophobicity analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: Productive localization of mitochondrial TA proteins is governed by an equilibrium between complex assembly and extraction of orphan subunits.
source: Based on these results, we suggest that productive localization of mitochondrial TA proteins is governed by an equilibrium between complex assembly and extraction of orphan subunits whereas Doa10 determines the cytoplasmic concentration of targeting competent species (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Doa10 determines the cytoplasmic concentration of targeting competent TA protein species.
source: Based on these results, we suggest that productive localization of mitochondrial TA proteins is governed by an equilibrium between complex assembly and extraction of orphan subunits whereas Doa10 determines the cytoplasmic concentration of targeting competent species (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Doa10 was initially identified in a screen for mutants with a defect in turnover of the soluble nuclear transcription factor MATα2.
source: Although Doa10 is a central player of ERAD (Mehrtash and Hochstrasser, 2018; Ruggiano et al., 2014), initially it has been identified in a screen for mutants with a defect in turnover of the soluble nuclear transcription factor MATα2 (Swanson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Doa10 has been linked to a pre-insertion ER quality control pathway of GPI-anchored proteins.
source: Consistent with this function in recognizing soluble proteins, it has been also linked to a pre-insertion ER quality control pathway of GPI-anchored proteins (Ast et al., 2014), which are commonly targeted to the Sec61 translocon post-translationally by an N-terminal SRP-independent signal sequence.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Doa10 samples and targets certain TA proteins prior their membrane insertion for proteasomal degradation distinct of its ERAD function.
source: Here, we now show that Doa10 samples and targets certain TA proteins prior their membrane insertion for proteasomal degradation distinct of its ERAD function.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Doa10 controls the cytosolic level of Fmp32 and Gem1 and regulates their OMM insertion.
source: However, certain key ERAD factors such as Cdc48 and Ubx2 were not analyzed in our screens because they were not present in our library (Li et al., 2011; Winzeler et al., 1999). While in the artificial Pex15-derived reporter (Pex15Δ30) we assume that the TM domain adopts a non-native conformation, we also show that the endogenous mitochondrial proteins Fmp32 and Gem1 are Doa10 substrates. This suggests, that Doa10 controls the cytosolic level of these proteins and by this regulates their OMM insertion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Fmp32 and Gem1 are Doa10 substrates.

claim: Targeting fidelity of TA proteins to cellular membranes is ensured by Doa10-dependent abundance control.
source: Therefore, we propose that targeting fidelity of TA proteins to cellular membranes is ensured by Doa10-dependent abundance control (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Full-length Pex15 protein only accumulates in the OMM upon compromised Msp1 function.
source: The full-length Pex15 protein only accumulates in the OMM upon compromised Msp1 function.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Doa10 deletion does not lead to a significant increase in cellular Pex15 level.
source: Doa10 deletion does not lead to a significant increase in cellular Pex15 level, indicating that it is a better client for the GET pathway and/or other peroxisomal targeting routes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Full-length Pex15 is a better client for the GET pathway and/or other peroxisomal targeting routes.
source: Doa10 deletion does not lead to a significant increase in cellular Pex15 level, indicating that it is a better client for the GET pathway and/or other peroxisomal targeting routes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of accumulation in doa10Δ.

claim: Microscopy analysis revealed substantial mitochondrial accumulation of Fmp32 in msp1Δ and doa10Δ strains.
source: In contrast, our microscopy analysis revealed substantial mitochondrial accumulation of Fmp32 in msp1Δ and doa10Δ strains.
evidence: This is a finding from microscopy analysis.

claim: The i-AAA protease Yme1 recognizes OMM proteins such as Tom22 and Om45 if they accidentally appear at the inner mitochondrial side.
source: In addition to dealing with proteins of the inner membrane, the active subunit of the i-AAA protease Yme1 has also been shown to recognize OMM proteins such as Tom22 and Om45 if they accidentally appear at the inner mitochondrial side (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Both Yme1 and Cdc48-mediated degradation require recognition of aberrant protein domains exposed into the intermembrane space or into the cytosol, respectively.
source: Given these powerful proteostasis factors, why do eukaryotic cells have an additional Msp1-dependent surveillance mechanism? One reason probably is that both Yme1 and Cdc48-mediated degradation require recognition of aberrant protein domains exposed into the intermembrane space or into the cytosol, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about these proteostasis factors.

claim: Msp1 completes surveillance of the OMM by recognizing TA proteins that do not possess any large C-terminal regions protruding into the intermembrane space nor contain any obvious folding defect in the cytoplasm.
source: Msp1 completes surveillance of the OMM by recognizing TA proteins that do not possess any large C-terminal regions protruding into the intermembrane space nor contain any obvious folding defect in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Interaction of Pex15 with the peroxisomal protein Pex3 is the determinant that prevents Msp1-mediated extraction.
source: A live cell quantitative microscopy approach combined with a computational analysis of Msp1 in peroxisomes suggested that interaction of Pex15 with the peroxisomal protein Pex3 is the determinant that prevents Msp1-mediated extraction (Weir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Only monomeric forms of the Pex15 TM domain reporter can be extracted by Msp1.
source: By applying chemical-induced dimerization to a mitochondria-localized Pex15 TM domain reporter we could show that only monomeric forms can be extracted by Msp1 even though both Doa10-mediated degradation and Msp1 are functional.
evidence: This is a finding from the dimerization experiments.

claim: Overexpressed Gem1 becomes a Msp1 client when its native complex partners are limiting.
source: Likewise, we observe that the overexpressed TA protein Gem1 becomes a Msp1 client when its native complex partners are limiting.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Msp1 samples the OMM and extracts monomeric TA proteins, whereas complex assembly counteracts this reaction.
source: Thus, we propose that Msp1 samples the OMM and extracts monomeric TA proteins, whereas complex assembly counteracts this reaction.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Extraction by Msp1 may be prevented by a steric clash of bulky cytoplasmic/IMS domains of the dimeric client protein or by the tandem TM segments exceeding the pulling force of the Msp1 dislocase.
source: Extraction may either be prevented by a steric clash of bulky cytoplasmic/IMS domains of the dimeric client protein or by the tandem TM segments exceeding the pulling force of the Msp1 dislocase.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how complex assembly prevents extraction.

claim: Msp1 acts as a membrane-anchored ATP-dependent ring hexamer with client proteins likely being extracted through the pore.
source: Interestingly, a recent biochemical and structural analysis revealed that Msp1 acts as a membrane-anchored ATP-dependent ring hexamer with client proteins likely being extracted through the pore (Wohlever et al., 2017).
evidence: This is knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Msp1 does not sample TM domains of clients.
source: Consistent with the idea that Msp1 does not sample TM domains of clients, we and others revealed that Msp1 extracts a heterogenous set of TA proteins lacking any obvious similarity in their TM anchors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) (Chen et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of similarity in TM anchors of Msp1 clients.

claim: The extent of OMM anchoring and/or complex assembly are important parameters for Msp1 recognition.
source: However, the extent of OMM anchoring and/or complex assembly are important parameters.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Cis1 is not required for the extraction of OMM TA proteins.
source: Of note, our genetic screen and a recent study (Li et al., 2019) imply that Cis1 is not required for the extraction of OMM TA proteins, revealing that Msp1 is a versatile dislocase that is used for multiple purposes.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic screen and supported by a citation.

claim: Msp1 is a versatile dislocase that is used for multiple purposes.
source: Of note, our genetic screen and a recent study (Li et al., 2019) imply that Cis1 is not required for the extraction of OMM TA proteins, revealing that Msp1 is a versatile dislocase that is used for multiple purposes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: The ER-localized chaperone Djp1 retrieves inner mitochondrial membrane proteins from the ER surface.
source: Taken together with a recent report on an ER surface retrieval pathway for inner mitochondrial membrane proteins by the ER-localized chaperone Djp1 (Hansen et al., 2018), our study reveals a so far unanticipated close interplay between these two organelles controlling protein abundance and targeting fidelity.
evidence: This is knowledge from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: There is a close interplay between the ER and mitochondria controlling protein abundance and targeting fidelity.
source: Taken together with a recent report on an ER surface retrieval pathway for inner mitochondrial membrane proteins by the ER-localized chaperone Djp1 (Hansen et al., 2018), our study reveals a so far unanticipated close interplay between these two organelles controlling protein abundance and targeting fidelity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings and a recent report.

claim: Control of complex assembly by potent mechanisms removing orphan subunits emerges as a widely used principle.
source: More generally, control of complex assembly by potent mechanisms removing orphan subunits emerges as a widely used principle (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Degradation of unassembled subunits in the cytoplasm and the ER is directly linked to E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: However, while degradation of unassembled subunits in the cytoplasm and the ER is directly linked to E3 ubiquitin ligases, Msp1 appears to act relatively unspecific.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Msp1 appears to act relatively unspecific.
source: However, while degradation of unassembled subunits in the cytoplasm and the ER is directly linked to E3 ubiquitin ligases, Msp1 appears to act relatively unspecific.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Doa10 samples insertion competent TA proteins to ensure their targeting fidelity, possibly preventing endless futile cycles of insertion and extraction.
source: In a separate process, Doa10 samples insertion competent TA proteins to ensure their targeting fidelity, possibly preventing endless futile cycles of insertion and extraction.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Homologues for Msp1 (ATAD1/Thorase) and Doa10 (MARCH6/TEB4) exist in humans.
source: Homologues for Msp1 (ATAD1/Thorase) and Doa10 (MARCH6/TEB4) exist in humans, indicating a conserved role of both proteostasis factors in the abundance and quality control of mitochondrial TA proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Msp1 and Doa10 have a conserved role in the abundance and quality control of mitochondrial TA proteins.
source: Homologues for Msp1 (ATAD1/Thorase) and Doa10 (MARCH6/TEB4) exist in humans, indicating a conserved role of both proteostasis factors in the abundance and quality control of mitochondrial TA proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the existence of human homologues and the findings of the study.
